context_html: We <u>could of</u> caught the earlier bus if the drills had ended on time.
stem_md: Which choice is the correct form of the verb phrase?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Of' is a preposition — it can't help a verb.
per_choice_rationale.B: The helper is 'have': could have caught.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Off' makes it worse, not better.
per_choice_rationale.D: Dropping the helper changes the meaning from missed chance to plain ability.

why_correct_md: The contraction 'could've' spells out as **could have** — never 'could of'.
why_tempted_md: 'Could've' SOUNDS exactly like 'could of'.
rule_md: Would/could/should pair with HAVE; the '-of' spelling is always an ear-spelling error.

context_html: The mural committee wanted a design that was not only colorful <u>but</u> durable enough for the north wall.
stem_md: Which choice completes the paired conjunction correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Not only' promises its full partner — bare 'but' breaks the pair.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Not only ... but also' is the complete correlative pair.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'And also' isn't the partner 'not only' takes.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Yet' signals contrast, and the pair still goes unfinished.

why_correct_md: Correlative conjunctions come in **fixed pairs**: not only ... but also.
why_tempted_md: 'But' alone carries most of the meaning, so the missing 'also' is easy to drop.
rule_md: Complete the pair: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also.

context_html: You can <u>either submit the form online or</u> mail it to the district office.
stem_md: Which choice places the paired conjunction so the options match?

choices.label: submit the form either online or
either submit the form online, or
submit either the form online or

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Either' sits before the verb but 'or' introduces only a place — the halves don't match.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Either online or [by] mail' — both arms of the pair now offer the same kind of thing.
per_choice_rationale.C: The mismatch stays, and the comma adds nothing.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Either the form' pairs a noun with a place — still lopsided.

why_correct_md: Place correlatives so the words after each arm are **grammatically parallel**.
why_tempted_md: The sentence sounds fine aloud because the meaning is guessable.
rule_md: Whatever follows 'either' must mirror what follows 'or' — noun/noun, verb/verb, place/place.

context_html: Last night the power flickered twice, and the smoke alarm <u>chirps</u> until Dad changed its battery.
stem_md: Which choice keeps the sentence in one time frame?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Last night' and 'changed' set the past — present 'chirps' jumps the track.
per_choice_rationale.B: Past 'chirped' matches 'flickered' and 'changed'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Chirping' leaves the clause without a real verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: Future tense contradicts a finished story.

why_correct_md: Stay in the tense the sentence establishes — here, the **past**.
why_tempted_md: The alarm's chirping is easy to picture as happening 'now'.
rule_md: Match every verb to the sentence's time markers unless the meaning truly changes time.

context_html: Every morning the ferry leaves at six, crosses the sound in forty minutes, and <u>docked</u> beside the fish market.
stem_md: Which choice keeps the daily routine consistent?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Docked' drops one leg of a present-tense routine into the past.
per_choice_rationale.B: Present 'docks' matches 'leaves' and 'crosses' — a habit, not a memory.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Was docking' shifts to a past scene mid-list.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Had docked' reaches even further back than the plain past.

why_correct_md: A routine described in present tense keeps **every verb present**.
why_tempted_md: Any single leg of the trip can be remembered as a past event.
rule_md: Verbs in a series share the sentence's time frame — don't shift without a reason.

context_html: By the time the bus finally arrived, Maria <u>waits</u> at the corner for over an hour.
stem_md: Which verb form best completes the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Present-tense 'waits' clashes with the past-tense 'arrived' that anchors the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Had been waiting' places the hour of waiting BEFORE the past arrival — exactly the sequence the sentence describes.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Is waiting' is present tense; the arrival already happened.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Will wait' pushes the waiting into the future, after the bus arrived — backwards.

why_correct_md: An action ongoing **before** a past event takes the past perfect (progressive): *had been waiting*.
why_tempted_md: Each verb form sounds fine alone; only checking it against 'arrived' exposes the clash.
rule_md: Match verb tense to the sentence's time anchors; 'by the time X happened' demands past perfect.

context_html: By the time we reached the trailhead, the sun had already <u>rose</u> over the ridge.
stem_md: Which choice is the correct form after 'had'?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Rose' is the simple past — 'had' needs the past participle.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Had risen' pairs the helper with the participle.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Rised' isn't a form of this irregular verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Raised' comes from 'raise' (to lift something) — the sun rises on its own.

why_correct_md: After 'had', irregular verbs use their **past participle**: had risen.
why_tempted_md: The simple past 'rose' is the form we say most often.
rule_md: Rise-rose-risen; raise-raised-raised. Helpers (have/had) take the third form.

context_html: I <u>seen</u> the meteor shower from the roof of the parking garage.
stem_md: Which choice is the correct past form of the verb?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Seen' is a participle — it can't stand alone without 'have' or 'had'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Saw' is the simple past and needs no helper.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Have saw' pairs the helper with the wrong form.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Seed' isn't a verb form at all here.

why_correct_md: Alone, the past of 'see' is **saw**; 'seen' only works with a helper.
why_tempted_md: 'I seen it' is common in casual speech.
rule_md: See-saw-seen: 'saw' stands alone; 'seen' rides with have/has/had.

context_html: Yesterday the choir <u>sung</u> the national anthem before the game.
stem_md: Which verb form is correct in this sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Sung' is the past participle and needs a helping verb ('had sung'); alone it cannot serve as the simple past.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Sang' is the simple past of 'sing' — exactly what 'Yesterday' calls for.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Singed' means lightly burned; it is not a form of 'sing'.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Sings' is present tense, clashing with 'Yesterday'.

why_correct_md: Irregular verb: sing → **sang** (simple past) → sung (participle, needs a helper).
why_tempted_md: 'Sung' sounds vaguely past-tense, and the sung/sang pair is easy to swap.
rule_md: Use the simple past form alone; save the participle (sung, swum, begun) for perfect tenses with 'have/had'.

context_html: The second week of practice went <u>more smooth</u> than the first.
stem_md: Which choice compares the two weeks correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Went' needs an adverb — 'smooth' is the adjective.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'More smoothly' is the comparative ADVERB the verb needs.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Smoother' compares two nouns, but here we're describing how practice WENT.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Most' is the superlative — there are only two weeks.

why_correct_md: Comparing how something happened takes a **comparative adverb**: more smoothly.
why_tempted_md: 'Smooth' and 'smoother' sound fine because the adjective is so familiar.
rule_md: Modify a verb with an adverb; compare two with 'more + adverb', not the bare adjective.

context_html: Of the two routes up the mountain, the eastern trail is the <u>most</u> challenging.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for comparing the two routes?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Most' is the superlative — it needs three or more routes to pick from.
per_choice_rationale.B: Exactly two things compare with the comparative: the eastern trail is the MORE challenging of the two.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'The much challenging' is not idiomatic before a bare adjective.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Very challenging' drops the comparison the sentence explicitly sets up.

why_correct_md: Two items → **comparative** ('more'); three or more → superlative ('most').
why_tempted_md: Superlatives are so common in speech that 'most challenging' sounds natural even for a pair.
rule_md: With exactly two things, use -er/'more'; save -est/'most' for three or more.

context_html: Switching to the aluminum bat made Dev's swing <u>more faster</u> through the strike zone.
stem_md: Which choice states the comparison without doubling it?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'More faster' marks the comparison twice — once with 'more', once with '-er'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Faster' carries the whole comparison in one form.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'More fast' uses the wrong marker for a one-syllable adjective.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Fastest' is the superlative — only two swings are being compared.

why_correct_md: Use **one** comparative marker: -er OR 'more', never both.
why_tempted_md: Doubling the marker feels like extra emphasis.
rule_md: Short adjectives take -er/-est; longer ones take more/most; never stack the two.

context_html: The understudy performed so <u>good</u> on opening night that the director rewrote the schedule.
stem_md: Which choice correctly describes how the understudy performed?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Good' is an adjective; 'performed' needs an adverb.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Well' is the adverb that tells HOW she performed.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Goodly' is archaic and means 'sizable', not 'skillfully'.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Great' is another adjective in an adverb's slot.

why_correct_md: Describe a verb with an **adverb**: performed well.
why_tempted_md: 'Did good' is everywhere in casual speech.
rule_md: Good describes nouns; well describes verbs (except health: 'I feel well').

context_html: Peanut butter and jelly <u>makes</u> a decent trail lunch when the cooler ice runs out.
stem_md: Which choice agrees with the compound subject?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two foods joined by 'and' form a plural subject — 'makes' is singular.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'And' builds a plural subject, and 'make' agrees with it.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Is making' is still singular and adds a progressive the sentence doesn't need.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Has made' is singular and shifts the general claim into a finished past.

why_correct_md: Subjects joined by **'and' are plural** — they take a plural verb.
why_tempted_md: The pair feels like one sandwich, so a singular verb sounds natural.
rule_md: X and Y → plural verb, unless the pair names a single fixed unit (macaroni and cheese IS).

context_html: The box of winter clothes <u>were</u> stored in the attic all summer.
stem_md: Which choice makes the subject and verb agree?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Were' agrees with the nearby plural 'clothes', but the subject is the singular 'box'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Have been' is also plural — same trap, plus a tense shift the sentence doesn't need.
per_choice_rationale.C: The subject is 'box' (singular); 'was' agrees with it.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Are' is plural AND present tense; the sentence describes the past summer.

why_correct_md: The verb agrees with the head noun **box**, not with the closer noun in the 'of' phrase.
why_tempted_md: The plural 'clothes' sits right next to the verb, luring the ear toward 'were'.
rule_md: Strip the prepositional phrase to find the true subject before choosing the verb.

context_html: Each of the drones <u>carry</u> a spare battery clipped beneath its frame.
stem_md: Which verb agrees with the subject of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: The subject is 'each', not 'drones' — and 'each' is singular.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Each' takes a singular verb no matter what plural follows 'of'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Are carrying' agrees with the nearby plural, not the actual subject.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Have carried' is plural and abandons the present-tense description.

why_correct_md: **'Each' is singular** — the 'of the drones' phrase can't change that.
why_tempted_md: The plural noun sits right next to the verb and pulls it plural.
rule_md: Indefinite pronouns each/either/neither/everyone are singular; ignore the 'of the ___' phrase.

context_html: Neither the captain nor the deckhands <u>was</u> willing to predict when the fog would lift.
stem_md: Which verb is correct after the 'neither ... nor' pair?

per_choice_rationale.A: With 'nor', the verb agrees with the CLOSER subject — plural 'deckhands'.
per_choice_rationale.B: The nearer subject is plural, so the verb goes plural: 'the deckhands were'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Is' is singular and drifts into present tense besides.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Has been' agrees with the farther subject and changes the time frame.

why_correct_md: In either/or and neither/nor pairs, the verb agrees with the **nearer subject**.
why_tempted_md: 'Neither' sounds singular, so a singular verb feels automatic.
rule_md: Or/nor: match the verb to whichever subject sits closest to it.

context_html: The library extended <u>their</u> weekend hours during exam season.
stem_md: Which pronoun agrees with 'the library'?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Their' is plural, but 'the library' is one thing.
per_choice_rationale.B: Singular, non-person antecedent → 'its'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'It's' means 'it is' — not a possessive.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'There' points to a place; it can't possess hours.

why_correct_md: A singular thing takes the singular possessive **'its'**.
why_tempted_md: Organizations feel like the people inside them, so 'their' slips in.
rule_md: Match the pronoun to the antecedent's number: one library → its.

context_html: Each kayak in the rental fleet has <u>their</u> own numbered paddle.
stem_md: Which pronoun matches the word it stands for?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Each kayak' is singular; 'their' is plural.
per_choice_rationale.B: One kayak at a time → 'its' paddle.
per_choice_rationale.C: A kayak isn't a person.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'There' is a place word, not a possessive.

why_correct_md: 'Each' keeps the antecedent **singular** — one kayak, its paddle.
why_tempted_md: The plural 'fleet' nearby pulls the pronoun plural.
rule_md: Each/every + noun stays singular no matter what plural stands nearby.

context_html: Tighten the strap so the helmet doesn't come <u>lose</u> on the downhill.
stem_md: Which choice is the right word for the strap's problem?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Lose' is a verb (to misplace); the sentence needs a describing word.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Loose' (rhymes with 'goose') means not tight.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Loosen' is an action, and 'come loosen' isn't English.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Come lost' garbles the idiom 'come loose'.

why_correct_md: **Loose** = not tight; **lose** = to misplace or be defeated.
why_tempted_md: One letter apart and pronounced almost alike, the pair swaps constantly.
rule_md: Loose rhymes with goose (adjective); lose rhymes with snooze (verb).

context_html: The new policy will <u>affect</u> how employees request time off.
stem_md: Which choice uses the right word for the sentence's meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence — 'will affect how employees request time off' is already correct.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Effect' as a verb means to bring something about ('effect change'); it cannot take 'how employees request' as its object.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Will affects' stacks a conjugated verb after 'will', which requires the base form.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Will effected' is doubly wrong: wrong word and wrong form after 'will'.

why_correct_md: To influence something = **affect** (verb); the sentence already uses it correctly.
why_tempted_md: The affect/effect pair is so notorious that a correct 'affect' invites second-guessing.
rule_md: Affect = verb (to influence); effect = noun (a result) — and check before you 'fix' what isn't broken.

context_html: From the coach's silence after tryouts, the players <u>implied</u> that the roster would shrink.
stem_md: Which choice is the right verb for what the players did?

per_choice_rationale.A: Speakers imply; listeners infer. The players were on the receiving end.
per_choice_rationale.B: Drawing a conclusion from evidence is 'inferring'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Implicated' means shown to be involved in wrongdoing.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Applied' belongs to forms and ointments, not conclusions.

why_correct_md: The sender **implies**; the receiver **infers**.
why_tempted_md: The two verbs describe the same conversation from opposite ends.
rule_md: Imply = hint outward; infer = conclude inward. Ask which direction the meaning travels.

context_html: The volunteer <u>which</u> organized the coat drive spoke at Friday's assembly.
stem_md: Which choice correctly refers to the volunteer?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Which' refers to things, not people.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Who' refers to a person doing the action of the clause.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Whom' is the object form — but the volunteer is the one organizing.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'What' can't introduce a clause about a person.

why_correct_md: People take **who/whom**; things take which/that.
why_tempted_md: 'Which' feels formal enough to fit anywhere.
rule_md: Person → who (subject) / whom (object); thing → which/that.

context_html: The mentor <u>who</u> Amara credits for her scholarship still teaches night classes.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the person Amara credits?

per_choice_rationale.A: Inside the clause, Amara credits HIM — an object, so 'who' is the wrong case.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Whom' is the object of 'credits': Amara credits whom.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Which' can't refer to a person.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Whose' is possessive — nothing is owned here.

why_correct_md: Test with him/her: 'Amara credits HIM' → **whom**.
why_tempted_md: 'Who' sounds natural at the head of any clause about a person.
rule_md: He/she fits → who; him/her fits → whom.

context_html: Riders are prohibited <u>to bring</u> glass bottles onto the pool deck.
stem_md: Which choice completes the expression idiomatically?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Prohibited to bring' crosses idioms — 'forbidden TO' but 'prohibited FROM'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Prohibited from + -ing' is the fixed pairing.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Prohibited of' isn't an English pattern.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Against bring' mangles both the preposition and the verb form.

why_correct_md: The idiom is **prohibited from doing**, not 'prohibited to do'.
why_tempted_md: The parallel idiom 'forbidden to do' bleeds into this one.
rule_md: Learn preposition idioms as units: prohibited from, forbidden to, capable of, insist on.

context_html: The results were consistent <u>to</u> the team's hypothesis.
stem_md: Which choice completes the idiom correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: English pairs 'consistent' with 'with', never 'to'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consistent with' is the standard idiom.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Consistent for' is not an English idiom.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Consistent about' describes a person's habits, not agreement between findings and a hypothesis.

why_correct_md: Idioms are fixed pairings: **consistent with** is the only standard form here.
why_tempted_md: 'To' feels connective, and many adjectives do take 'to' (similar to, equal to).
rule_md: Learn preposition pairings as fixed units — 'consistent with', 'capable of', 'preoccupied with'.

context_html: The docent led us through the fossil hall, pointed out the juvenile triceratops, and <u>explains</u> how the dig team dated the site.
stem_md: Which choice keeps the tour's verbs consistent?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two past verbs then a present one — the last leg jumps time frames.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Explained' completes the past-tense series 'led ... pointed ... explained'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Explaining' breaks the parallel finite-verb series.
per_choice_rationale.D: Future tense contradicts a tour already being narrated.

why_correct_md: Verbs in one narrated sequence stay in **one tense**.
why_tempted_md: The explanation feels ongoing, so present tense sneaks in.
rule_md: Series of actions by one subject: keep every verb in the frame the first verbs set.

context_html: When one trains at altitude for a few weeks, <u>you</u> notice the difference at sea level immediately.
stem_md: Which choice keeps the sentence's point of view consistent?

per_choice_rationale.A: The sentence opens with 'one' and then swerves to 'you'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'One ... one notices' holds a single point of view.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'They' invents a third party the sentence never introduced.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'We noticed' changes both person and tense.

why_correct_md: Pick a person — 'one' or 'you' — and **stay in it**.
why_tempted_md: 'One' and 'you' both speak generally, so they feel interchangeable mid-sentence.
rule_md: Don't shift person (one → you → they) inside a sentence or passage.

context_html: By the time the judges reached our booth, the glue <u>dried</u> and the bridge model held its full load.
stem_md: Which choice shows the drying happened before the judges arrived?

per_choice_rationale.A: Plain past puts the drying and the arrival at the same moment.
per_choice_rationale.B: Past perfect 'had dried' sets the drying BEFORE the past arrival.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Has dried' ties the drying to the present, not to that past moment.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Was drying' means the glue was still wet — the opposite of the point.

why_correct_md: **Past perfect** ('had' + participle) marks the earlier of two past events.
why_tempted_md: Simple past feels sufficient because both events are over.
rule_md: 'By the time X happened, Y HAD happened' — the earlier past takes 'had'.

context_html: Jordan texted Marcus every day while <u>he</u> was at wilderness camp.
stem_md: Which choice makes clear who was away at camp?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'He' could be Jordan or Marcus — the reader can't tell who left.
per_choice_rationale.B: Repeating the name removes the ambiguity.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Him' is the wrong case for a subject and no clearer.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Himself' needs a matching subject in its own clause.

why_correct_md: When a pronoun could point at **either person**, use the name.
why_tempted_md: The writer knows who went to camp, so the pronoun feels clear.
rule_md: A pronoun must have exactly ONE possible antecedent — otherwise name the person.

context_html: The volunteer <u>whom</u> organized the food drive received an award.
stem_md: Which pronoun is correct here?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Whom' is an object pronoun, but this pronoun is the SUBJECT of 'organized'.
per_choice_rationale.B: The pronoun performs the verb 'organized', so the subject form 'who' is required.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Which' refers to things; the volunteer is a person.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Whose' shows possession — nothing is being possessed here.

why_correct_md: Subject of the verb → **who**; object of a verb or preposition → whom.
why_tempted_md: 'Whom' sounds more formal, so it gets sprinkled in where 'who' belongs.
rule_md: Test with he/him: 'HE organized the drive' → who; 'the drive was organized by HIM' → whom.

context_html: Any questions about the field trip should go to Ms. Rivera or <u>myself</u> before Friday.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the second contact person?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Myself' is reflexive — it needs 'I' earlier in the clause to reflect.
per_choice_rationale.B: Questions go TO someone: the object form 'me'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'I' is the subject form in an object slot.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Mine' shows possession, which nothing here calls for.

why_correct_md: No earlier 'I' to reflect → plain **me**, not 'myself'.
why_tempted_md: 'Myself' sounds extra polite in requests and announcements.
rule_md: Reflexives (-self) only echo a subject already in the clause: 'I hurt myself', never 'contact myself'.

context_html: Lena rehearsed her lines for weeks. <u>Similarly</u>, she froze the moment the curtain rose.
stem_md: Which transition correctly signals the contrast?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Similarly' promises more of the same, but freezing on stage contradicts weeks of rehearsal.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'However' names the real relationship: the outcome defied the preparation.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Likewise' makes the same false promise as 'Similarly'.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Therefore' claims freezing FOLLOWED LOGICALLY from rehearsing — backwards.

why_correct_md: The second sentence **contradicts** the expectation the first sets up — that's 'However'.
why_tempted_md: Any transition reads smoothly if you don't test the logical claim it makes.
rule_md: Name the actual relationship (contrast, cause, example, addition) before choosing a transition.

context_html: First, soak the beans overnight. <u>In other words</u>, rinse them and set them to simmer.
stem_md: Which transition fits the step-by-step sequence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In other words' promises a restatement, but rinsing and simmering are NEW steps, not the soaking rephrased.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'For instance' promises an example of soaking — rinsing isn't one.
per_choice_rationale.C: The passage is a sequence of steps; 'Next' moves it to step two.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In contrast' claims the steps oppose each other; they simply follow each other.

why_correct_md: Instructions advance step by step — the transition must mark **sequence**.
why_tempted_md: Restatement transitions sound explanatory, which feels helpful in instructions.
rule_md: In a procedure, use sequence transitions (first, next, then, finally) between steps.

context_html: Ella trained all winter for the marathon. <u>In contrast</u>, she finished in her best time ever.
stem_md: Which transition names the actual relationship between the sentences?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In contrast' promises opposition, but the best-ever finish FOLLOWS FROM the training.
per_choice_rationale.B: The record finish is the outcome of the winter of training — cause and effect.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For instance' promises an example, not an outcome.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'On the other hand' signals the same false contrast as 'In contrast'.

why_correct_md: The second sentence is the **result** of the first — the transition must say so.
why_tempted_md: Any transition reads smoothly if you don't test the logic it claims.
rule_md: Name the real relationship (cause, example, contrast, time) before picking a transition.

context_html: The trail was steep and poorly marked. <u>In fact</u>, the view from the summit repaid every step.
stem_md: Which transition acknowledges the concession the passage makes?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'In fact' intensifies what came before; the second sentence pivots away from the complaint instead.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Even so' concedes the hard climb, then asserts the reward despite it — exactly the move the passage makes.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'As a result' claims the great view was CAUSED by bad trail markings.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For example' promises an instance of steepness; a rewarding view isn't one.

why_correct_md: Hardship conceded, reward asserted anyway → a **concession** transition ('even so', 'nevertheless').
why_tempted_md: 'In fact' is a common intensifier, and the sentence pair reads fine until the logic is tested.
rule_md: When sentence two says 'despite that', the transition must carry the concession.

context_html: The library's archive holds thousands of rare maps. <u>Therefore</u>, its oldest map dates to 1502.
stem_md: Which transition best fits what the second sentence does?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' claims the 1502 map is a logical consequence of the archive's size — it isn't.
per_choice_rationale.B: The 1502 map is a specific illustration of the archive's rare holdings — an example.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'However' promises a contrast the sentences don't make.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In conclusion' signals a summary, but the sentence adds a new detail.

why_correct_md: A concrete instance supporting a general claim is introduced with **for example**.
why_tempted_md: 'Therefore' sounds authoritative, masking that nothing is actually being deduced.
rule_md: General claim followed by a specific instance → an example transition.

context_html: <u>Honey has been harvested for thousands of years.</u> Bees pollinate roughly a third of the crops humans eat, and almond growers truck hives across entire states each spring. Without managed colonies, many orchards would produce almost nothing.
stem_md: Which choice provides the best topic sentence for the paragraph?

choices.label: Beekeepers wear protective suits for good reason.
Honey comes in many colors and flavors.
Bees are essential partners in modern agriculture.

per_choice_rationale.A: The paragraph is about pollination and farming, not the history of honey harvesting.
per_choice_rationale.B: Protective suits never come up — the body is about crops and orchards.
per_choice_rationale.C: Honey varieties are irrelevant to pollination statistics and trucked hives.
per_choice_rationale.D: Every body sentence — the crop share, the trucked hives, the barren orchards — supports bees as agricultural partners.

why_correct_md: A topic sentence must be the claim **every body sentence supports**.
why_tempted_md: Honey feels on-topic because bees make it — adjacency masquerades as relevance.
rule_md: Read the body first; the right topic sentence is the one the details already argue for.

context_html: The essay opens with the image of the lighthouse dark and boarded up. It then recounts the two-year volunteer restoration. <u>Fundraising for the restoration ended in June.</u>
stem_md: The writer wants a conclusion that returns to the essay's opening image of the lighthouse. Which choice accomplishes this?

choices.label: Today the restored beacon sweeps the bay each night, just as it did in 1902.
Many coastal towns face similar budget shortfalls.
The preservation committee will meet again next spring.

per_choice_rationale.A: A fundraising date is administrative housekeeping — it never looks back at the lighthouse.
per_choice_rationale.B: The lit beacon sweeping the bay answers the opening's dark, boarded-up tower — the frame closes.
per_choice_rationale.C: Other towns' budgets point AWAY from this essay's subject entirely.
per_choice_rationale.D: A future meeting is logistics, not imagery.

why_correct_md: A framing conclusion must **revisit the opening image** — dark tower then, lit beacon now.
why_tempted_md: Factually true closers feel legitimate even when they ignore the stated goal.
rule_md: When the stem names the writer's goal, eliminate every choice that doesn't perform it — truth alone doesn't qualify.

context_html: A late frost destroyed half the orchard's trees<u>; consequently,</u> the annual cider festival went on as planned.
stem_md: Which transition matches the relationship between the frost and the festival?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Consequently' claims the festival happened BECAUSE of the frost — the frost worked against it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'For example' would make the festival an instance of frost damage, which it isn't.
per_choice_rationale.C: The festival proceeded DESPITE the destruction — 'nevertheless' carries exactly that defiance.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'In addition' stacks the festival on top of the frost as more of the same; they pull opposite ways.

why_correct_md: Setback + outcome-despite-it = **nevertheless**, not a cause-effect transition.
why_tempted_md: 'Consequently' sounds authoritative, and both sentences do describe real events in order.
rule_md: Ask whether the second clause happens because of, despite, or alongside the first — then pick the transition that says so.

context_html: The camping checklist included a tent<u> a lantern matches</u> and a first-aid kit.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the items in the series correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: With no commas, four separate supplies blur into one unreadable run.
per_choice_rationale.B: Commas separate each item in the series of four supplies.
per_choice_rationale.C: This leaves 'a lantern matches' fused into one item — a lantern isn't a kind of match.
per_choice_rationale.D: Semicolons separate series items only when the items already contain commas.

why_correct_md: Commas separate **every item** in a simple series.
why_tempted_md: Short items read fast aloud, so the missing commas are easy to skate past.
rule_md: In a series of three or more, put a comma after each item except the last.

context_html: My grandparents moved to Tucson<u> Arizona on March 4 1998</u> after the bakery closed.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the place and date correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: City-state pairs and day-year pairs both need commas to stay readable.
per_choice_rationale.B: Commas set off the state and the year on both sides — the full convention.
per_choice_rationale.C: The state needs a comma on BOTH sides, and the year needs its closing comma too.
per_choice_rationale.D: The state is handled, but the day and year are left fused.

why_correct_md: State names and years act like interrupters: **commas on both sides**.
why_tempted_md: The single comma before 'Arizona' looks like it is already doing the job.
rule_md: City, State, ... and Month Day, Year, ... — the state and the year each take a closing comma.

context_html: The tide was coming in fast<u> so</u> we dragged the kayaks up past the dune grass.
stem_md: Which choice correctly joins the two halves of the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two complete thoughts joined by 'so' need a comma before the conjunction.
per_choice_rationale.B: Comma + coordinating conjunction is the standard join for two independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon replaces the conjunction — using both, plus a stray comma, doubles the connector.
per_choice_rationale.D: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; the pause belongs before it.

why_correct_md: Independent clause + **comma + FANBOYS** + independent clause.
why_tempted_md: 'So' feels small enough to glue the halves together without help.
rule_md: Put the comma BEFORE a coordinating conjunction that joins two complete thoughts — never after it.

context_html: Because the storm had knocked out power across the valley<u> the</u> town meeting moved to the fire hall.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the boundary after the opening clause?

per_choice_rationale.A: A full dependent clause opens this sentence — running it straight into the main clause hides where one ends and the other begins.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma after an introductory dependent clause marks the boundary the reader needs.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon needs independent clauses on BOTH sides; 'Because ... valley' cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.D: A period strands 'Because the storm had knocked out power across the valley' as a fragment.

why_correct_md: An introductory dependent clause is set off from the main clause with a **comma**.
why_tempted_md: Read quickly aloud, the sentence seems to flow fine without any pause.
rule_md: A dependent clause that OPENS the sentence takes a comma before the main clause — 'Because X happened, Y followed.'

context_html: After three straight weekends of tryouts and scrimmages<u> the</u> coach finally posted the roster.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the sentence's opening correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: A long opening phrase runs straight into the main clause without a marked boundary.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma after the long introductory phrase shows where the main clause begins.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon needs a complete clause on its left — the opener has no verb.
per_choice_rationale.D: A colon needs a complete statement before it, and the opener isn't one.

why_correct_md: A **long introductory phrase** takes a comma before the main clause begins.
why_tempted_md: Openers without verbs feel too small to deserve punctuation.
rule_md: After a long opening phrase (four-plus words), set the main clause off with a comma.

context_html: She pulled on a <u>warm wool</u> sweater and stepped into the sleet.
stem_md: Which choice handles the adjectives before 'sweater' correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Warm' describes the wool sweater as a unit — stacked (cumulative) adjectives take no comma.
per_choice_rationale.B: The swap test fails ('wool warm sweater'?) — these adjectives aren't coordinate, so no comma.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma between the last adjective and its noun is never correct.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'And' only joins adjectives that could trade places — these can't.

why_correct_md: These adjectives **stack**: 'warm' modifies 'wool sweater' as a whole, so no comma.
why_tempted_md: Two adjectives in a row look like the comma-separated kind at a glance.
rule_md: Comma only between adjectives that pass the swap/'and' test; cumulative adjectives take none.

context_html: Our biology teacher<u>, Mr. Alvarez,</u> keeps a terrarium of hissing cockroaches behind his desk.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the teacher's name correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: The name merely renames 'our biology teacher', so a PAIR of commas sets it off.
per_choice_rationale.B: An interrupter needs commas on both sides — opening one without closing it splices the name into the verb.
per_choice_rationale.C: Closing the interrupter without opening it makes the comma look like it belongs to the verb phrase.
per_choice_rationale.D: With no commas the name reads as restrictive — as if several biology teachers had to be told apart.

why_correct_md: A renaming appositive is set off by a **pair of commas** — both sides or neither.
why_tempted_md: Only one pause is easy to hear aloud, so a single comma feels sufficient.
rule_md: A nonrestrictive appositive takes commas on BOTH sides; drop both only when the name truly restricts.

context_html: The lighthouse<u> built in 1902 by a crew of eleven</u> still guides boats through the narrows.
stem_md: Which choice sets off the phrase about the lighthouse's construction correctly?

choices.label: , built in 1902 by a crew of eleven,
, built in 1902 by a crew of eleven
that was built in 1902 by a crew of eleven,

per_choice_rationale.A: Extra history about an already-identified lighthouse needs to be set off.
per_choice_rationale.B: Paired commas mark the phrase as droppable background detail.
per_choice_rationale.C: The interrupter opens with a comma but never closes.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'That' frames the detail as restrictive — and still leaves one stray comma.

why_correct_md: The phrase adds droppable background about one specific lighthouse → **paired commas**.
why_tempted_md: The phrase sits so close to its noun that it feels built in.
rule_md: Nonrestrictive (extra) modifiers take commas on both sides; restrictive ones take none.

context_html: It was the current<u> not the wind</u> that pushed the raft off course.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the contrast correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: The 'not X' contrast is an interrupter and can't run bare into the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Antithetical phrases are set off by commas on BOTH sides.
per_choice_rationale.C: Dropping the closing comma splices the contrast into 'that'.
per_choice_rationale.D: An opening dash with no closing partner leaves the frame unmatched.

why_correct_md: An antithetical phrase ('not the wind') is set off by a **pair of commas**.
why_tempted_md: The sentence reads smoothly with only the first comma's pause.
rule_md: Contrastive 'not X' interrupters take commas before AND after.

context_html: The robotics club renamed <u>it's</u> entry an hour before the qualifying round.
stem_md: Which choice is correct before 'entry'?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'It's' means 'it is' — and 'renamed it is entry' collapses.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Its' is the possessive form, written with no apostrophe.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Its'' is not a word in any position.
per_choice_rationale.D: Expanding the contraction proves it wrong: 'renamed it is entry'.

why_correct_md: Possessive 'its' takes **no apostrophe** — the apostrophe version always means 'it is'.
why_tempted_md: Most possessives DO take apostrophes, so 'it's' looks right.
rule_md: Test by expanding: if 'it is' fails in the slot, write 'its'.

context_html: Rex pulled hard, and the <u>dogs'</u> leash slipped from Maya's hand.
stem_md: Which choice makes the possessive correct?

per_choice_rationale.A: The apostrophe after the s marks a plural possessive, but only one dog — Rex — is in the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: One dog owns the leash, so the singular possessive 'dog's' is correct.
per_choice_rationale.C: Without an apostrophe there is no possessive at all — the leash must belong to the dog.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'dogss'' is not a word form in English.

why_correct_md: One owner → apostrophe **before** the s: *dog's*.
why_tempted_md: Plural and possessive forms sound identical aloud, so the written apostrophe placement is easy to miss.
rule_md: Singular owner → 's; plural owners ending in s → s'.

context_html: Whiskers meowed until Maya filled the <u>cats</u> bowl.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the possessive correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: Without an apostrophe, 'cats' is just a plural — nothing shows the bowl belongs to the cat.
per_choice_rationale.B: The apostrophe after the s claims several cats own the bowl, but only Whiskers is in the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: One cat — Whiskers — owns the bowl, so the singular possessive 'cat's' is correct.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'cats's' is not a standard English form.

why_correct_md: One owner → apostrophe **before** the s: *cat's*.
why_tempted_md: Plural 'cats' and possessive 'cat's' sound identical aloud, so the missing apostrophe is easy to overlook.
rule_md: Singular owner → 's; plural owners ending in s → s'.

context_html: Both <u>coach's</u> agreed the schedule left too little time for warm-ups.
stem_md: Which choice writes the word for two coaches correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: Apostrophe-s builds a possessive, but nothing in the sentence is owned.
per_choice_rationale.B: A plain plural takes -es and no apostrophe.
per_choice_rationale.C: The plural possessive still needs something possessed — there's nothing here.
per_choice_rationale.D: Nouns ending in -ch form their plurals with -es.

why_correct_md: 'Both' just means two of them — a **plural**, no apostrophe.
why_tempted_md: Apostrophes creep in whenever a noun ends in an s-sound.
rule_md: Apostrophes mark possession or contraction — never a plain plural.

context_html: <u>Maya and Jonah's</u> podcast about minor-league mascots just passed a hundred episodes.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the podcast the two friends share?

per_choice_rationale.A: One shared podcast → the apostrophe hangs on the LAST owner only.
per_choice_rationale.B: Separate apostrophes would signal two separate podcasts.
per_choice_rationale.C: This marks the first owner and strands the second entirely.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Jonahs'' treats the name as a plural that doesn't exist.

why_correct_md: Joint ownership hangs ONE apostrophe on the **final owner**.
why_tempted_md: Two owners feel like they deserve two apostrophes.
rule_md: Shared thing → apostrophe on the last name; separate things → apostrophe on each name.

context_html: The <u>dancers costumes</u> hung along the mirror wall, each tagged with a scene number.
stem_md: Which choice shows that the costumes belong to the dancers?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two plain nouns in a row leave the ownership unmarked.
per_choice_rationale.B: A plural owner ending in s takes its apostrophe after the s.
per_choice_rationale.C: This puts every costume in the hands of a single dancer.
per_choice_rationale.D: Adding 's after a plural s ('dancers's') is never correct.

why_correct_md: Plural owners that already end in s add **just the apostrophe**.
why_tempted_md: The singular 's pattern is so common it gets pasted onto plurals.
rule_md: Singular owner → 's; plural owners ending in s → s' (apostrophe alone).

context_html: The judges compared <u>Priya and Marcus's</u> essays before choosing a winner.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for essays each student wrote separately?

per_choice_rationale.A: A single apostrophe on the last name claims one co-written set of essays.
per_choice_rationale.B: Separately owned essays give EACH owner an apostrophe.
per_choice_rationale.C: Still one owner marked — and 'Marcus'' drops the s his singular name needs.
per_choice_rationale.D: The second owner is left with no possessive at all.

why_correct_md: Separately owned things give **each owner** an apostrophe.
why_tempted_md: The joint-ownership pattern (last name only) gets over-applied to every pair.
rule_md: Ask shared-or-separate: shared → last owner only; separate → every owner marked.

context_html: The <u>childrens'</u> mural stretches down the hallway outside the art room.
stem_md: Which choice is the correct possessive for the young artists?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Childrens' isn't a word — the apostrophe lands after a fake plural.
per_choice_rationale.B: Irregular plurals form possessives with 's, just like singulars.
per_choice_rationale.C: No apostrophe means no possession, and the fake plural remains.
per_choice_rationale.D: The bare plural drops the ownership the sentence asserts.

why_correct_md: Irregular plurals (children, women, mice) form possessives with **'s**, not s'.
why_tempted_md: The plural-ends-in-s rule (s') gets forced onto plurals that never end in s.
rule_md: If the plural doesn't end in s, add 's: children's, women's, geese's.

context_html: Marcus finished the marathon<u>, his</u> sister cheered from the finish line.
stem_md: Which choice best joins the two independent clauses?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: A colon promises that the second clause explains or expands the first; the sister's cheering is a separate event, not an explanation.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon plus 'and,' piles two joiners (and a stray comma) where one is needed.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon is the standard way to join two closely related independent clauses.

why_correct_md: Two related independent clauses join with a **semicolon** when no conjunction is used.
why_tempted_md: The comma splice reads smoothly aloud, so the error hides in plain sight.
rule_md: Independent clause + independent clause → semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction — never a comma alone.

context_html: The recipe calls for three <u>ingredients flour</u>, sugar, and butter.
stem_md: Which choice correctly punctuates the introduction of the list?

per_choice_rationale.A: With no punctuation, the list runs into the noun it names — readers can't tell where 'ingredients' ends and the list begins.
per_choice_rationale.B: A colon after a complete statement introduces the list it promises: three ingredients — then names them.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon separates two independent clauses; it cannot introduce a list.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'ingredients'' adds a possessive apostrophe nothing in the sentence calls for.

why_correct_md: A **colon** follows a complete statement to introduce the list it announces.
why_tempted_md: The sentence reads smoothly aloud, so the missing punctuation is easy to skate past.
rule_md: Use a colon — never a semicolon — after a complete clause to introduce a list.

context_html: Rehearsal ran long<u>, however,</u> nobody left before the final scene was blocked.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates 'however' between the two statements correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'However' between commas can't hold two clauses together — that's still a splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Semicolon before and comma after is how 'however' bridges two clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: The comma 'however' takes after itself is missing.
per_choice_rationale.D: The marks are reversed — the heavy mark goes before the bridge word.

why_correct_md: Clause **; however,** clause — semicolon before, comma after.
why_tempted_md: 'However' feels like 'but', which really does take just a comma.
rule_md: Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, meanwhile) joining clauses take ';' before and ',' after.

context_html: The storm knocked out the scoreboard<u>, the</u> referees kept score on a clipboard.
stem_md: Which choice repairs the join between the two statements?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone can't hold two complete thoughts together.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon joins the two closely related independent clauses.
per_choice_rationale.C: Removing the comma fuses the sentences outright.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'So' would need a comma before it; bare, it just smears the join.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses with no conjunction take a **semicolon**.
why_tempted_md: The clauses are so tightly related that a comma feels sufficient.
rule_md: Comma-splice fixes: semicolon, period, or comma + FANBOYS — never a comma alone.

context_html: Every camper packs the same three essentials<u>;</u> water, sun protection, and a whistle.
stem_md: Which punctuation mark belongs before the list of essentials?

per_choice_rationale.A: A semicolon needs a complete clause on each side — a list isn't one.
per_choice_rationale.B: The complete statement hands off to its promised list with a colon.
per_choice_rationale.C: A comma tangles the list into the clause that announces it.
per_choice_rationale.D: A period strands the list as a fragment.

why_correct_md: Complete statement + list → **colon** delivers the items the sentence promised.
why_tempted_md: Semicolons and colons blur together as 'formal marks before lists'.
rule_md: A colon introduces a list only after a complete statement; a semicolon never introduces a list.

context_html: After the blackout, the theater made one change<u>; battery-powered</u> exit signs in every stairwell.
stem_md: Which choice correctly introduces what the change was?

per_choice_rationale.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides — the right side is a phrase.
per_choice_rationale.B: The colon presents the change the clause just promised.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'It added ...' after only a comma splices two clauses.
per_choice_rationale.D: Fusing leaves 'change battery-powered exit signs' unreadable.

why_correct_md: A complete clause announcing something hands off with a **colon** — even to a phrase.
why_tempted_md: Semicolon and colon look interchangeable at the pivot of a sentence.
rule_md: Colon: complete clause before, anything after. Semicolon: complete clauses on BOTH sides.

context_html: The debate team traveled to Austin<u>, Texas, Portland,</u> Oregon, and Boise, Idaho for the spring circuit.
stem_md: Which choice keeps the three city-state pairs distinct?

per_choice_rationale.A: All-commas makes 'Texas' and 'Portland' read as two separate stops.
per_choice_rationale.B: Semicolons separate series items that already contain commas.
per_choice_rationale.C: This splits a city from its own state.
per_choice_rationale.D: A colon can't separate items in a series.

why_correct_md: When series items contain commas, **semicolons** separate the items.
why_tempted_md: Plain commas are the series habit even after the items grow internal commas.
rule_md: Upgrade series separators to semicolons once any item has an internal comma.

context_html: The judges announced that the three finalists <u>are: a baker from Reno, a chef from Tulsa,</u> and a caterer from Boise.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the introduction of the finalists correctly?

choices.label: are a baker from Reno, a chef from Tulsa,
are: a baker from Reno; a chef from Tulsa;
are; a baker from Reno, a chef from Tulsa,

per_choice_rationale.A: The colon interrupts 'are' and its complement — the clause before a colon must be complete.
per_choice_rationale.B: The list completes the verb directly; no punctuation belongs between 'are' and what the finalists are.
per_choice_rationale.C: This keeps the illegal colon and adds semicolons these short, comma-free items never need.
per_choice_rationale.D: A semicolon after 'are' cuts the clause off from its own complement.

why_correct_md: 'Are' already introduces the list — **no punctuation** sits between a verb and its complement.
why_tempted_md: Colons DO introduce lists — just not when the words before the colon can't stand alone.
rule_md: Use a colon only after a COMPLETE statement; never right after 'are', 'include', or 'such as'.

context_html: Two of the printers jammed before first period<u>,</u> the third ran out of toner by lunch.
stem_md: Which mark correctly separates the two printer problems?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone splices two complete statements.
per_choice_rationale.B: A semicolon pairs the two related, parallel failures.
per_choice_rationale.C: A colon promises that the second clause explains the first — it only adds a parallel mishap.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Moreover' after a comma is still a splice; it would need a semicolon in front.

why_correct_md: Related complete statements joined without a conjunction take a **semicolon**.
why_tempted_md: The clauses are short and parallel, so the comma feels light and quick.
rule_md: Semicolon = related independent clauses, no conjunction; colon = only when the second part explains the first.

context_html: Mr. Okafor<u>, he is the school's athletic trainer,</u> keeps a scrapbook of every season since 1998.
stem_md: Which choice correctly folds the trainer detail into the sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Mr. Okafor, he is ...' jams a whole clause where an appositive belongs.
per_choice_rationale.B: The bare noun phrase renames him cleanly between commas.
per_choice_rationale.C: Without commas, the phrase collides with the name it renames.
per_choice_rationale.D: Doubling the subject doubles the clutter.

why_correct_md: To tuck a fact inside a sentence, use an **appositive phrase**, not a full clause.
why_tempted_md: The original clause is perfectly grammatical — just not inside another sentence.
rule_md: Rename with a comma-wrapped phrase; save 'he is' for a separate sentence.

context_html: The trail's last water source <u>(a spring that runs dry by August</u> sits two miles below the summit.
stem_md: Which choice handles the parenthetical about the spring correctly?

choices.label: (a spring that runs dry by August)
a spring that runs dry by August)
(a spring that runs dry by August,

per_choice_rationale.A: The opening parenthesis never closes.
per_choice_rationale.B: Parentheses close what they open — the aside is sealed on both ends.
per_choice_rationale.C: This closes an aside that never opened.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma can't stand in for the closing parenthesis.

why_correct_md: **Parentheses travel in pairs** — every opener needs its closer.
why_tempted_md: By the end of a long aside it's easy to forget the bracket is still open.
rule_md: Whatever opens an aside (comma, dash, parenthesis) must be matched at its close.

context_html: The final stretch of the relay<u> the part everyone dreads </u>is a hill with no shade.
stem_md: Which choice sets off the aside about the relay correctly?

per_choice_rationale.A: The aside needs marks to lift it out of the main sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: Matched dashes frame the interruption on both sides.
per_choice_rationale.C: A dash that opens can't be closed by a comma.
per_choice_rationale.D: A comma that opens can't be closed by a dash.

why_correct_md: An abrupt aside takes **matched dashes** — the same mark on both sides.
why_tempted_md: One dash feels dramatic enough, and the closing partner gets forgotten.
rule_md: Interrupters pair their marks: two commas, two dashes, or two parentheses — never a mix.

context_html: Seeds<u>, that</u> sprout in the cold frame get moved to the garden after the last frost.
stem_md: Which choice is correct for the seeds being singled out?

per_choice_rationale.A: The comma + 'that' contradicts itself — 'that' clauses are never set off.
per_choice_rationale.B: Restrictive 'that' with no comma picks out WHICH seeds get moved.
per_choice_rationale.C: ', which' makes the detail optional — then ALL seeds get moved, changing the claim.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Which' with a stray trailing comma is neither restrictive nor properly nonrestrictive.

why_correct_md: The clause **restricts** — only the cold-frame sprouters move — so: 'that', no comma.
why_tempted_md: 'Which' sounds more formal, and commas feel polite around any clause.
rule_md: Restrictive → 'that', no commas. Nonrestrictive → ', which ..., ' with commas.

context_html: My cousin Leah<u> who taught herself to juggle during a rain delay</u> now performs between innings.
stem_md: Which choice punctuates the detail about Leah correctly?

choices.label: , who taught herself to juggle during a rain delay,
, who taught herself to juggle during a rain delay
that taught herself to juggle during a rain delay

per_choice_rationale.A: Leah is already identified by name — the extra story needs setting off.
per_choice_rationale.B: Paired commas mark the clause as droppable detail about a named person.
per_choice_rationale.C: The aside opens but never closes.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'That' for a person, and restrictive framing for someone already named — wrong twice.

why_correct_md: A clause adding detail about a **named person** is nonrestrictive: commas on both sides.
why_tempted_md: Read quickly, nothing looks broken without the commas.
rule_md: If the noun is already fully identified, the clause is extra — set it off with commas.

context_html: Passengers<u>, who checked bags,</u> should proceed to carousel four.
stem_md: Which choice tells only the right passengers to go to carousel four?

per_choice_rationale.A: The commas make the clause apply to ALL passengers — everyone gets sent to the carousel.
per_choice_rationale.B: The restrictive clause limits the instruction to passengers who checked bags.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Which' can't refer to people, and the commas still over-include.
per_choice_rationale.D: The half-converted participle drags a stray comma with it.

why_correct_md: Dropping the commas makes the clause **restrictive** — only those passengers.
why_tempted_md: Commas feel harmless, but here they change who is being addressed.
rule_md: Commas around the clause = applies to all; no commas = only those. Punctuate the MEANING.

context_html: The lifeguard <u>swam</u> toward the struggling swimmer.
stem_md: The writer wants to emphasize the speed of the rescue. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Swam' is accurate but neutral — it says nothing about speed.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Sprinted through the surf' is vivid and fast — exactly the urgency the writer wants.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Made her way' is leisurely, the opposite of urgent.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Eventually paddled' makes the rescue sound slow and reluctant.

why_correct_md: When the stem states the writer's goal, pick the choice that **delivers that goal** most strongly.
why_tempted_md: Accurate-but-bland options like 'swam' feel safe because nothing is wrong with them grammatically.
rule_md: Goal questions are not grammar questions — grade each choice against the stated purpose alone.

context_html: Dr. Okafor became <u>notorious</u> for her groundbreaking vaccine research.
stem_md: Which word carries the connotation the sentence needs?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Notorious' means famous for something BAD — it slanders the research it means to praise.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Infamous' has the same negative charge as 'notorious'.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Renowned' is fame with a positive glow — right for groundbreaking research.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Suspected' implies wrongdoing that the sentence never mentions.

why_correct_md: Denotation is 'famous'; the needed **connotation** is positive → *renowned*.
why_tempted_md: 'Notorious' sounds impressive and vaguely means 'well-known'.
rule_md: Check a word's emotional charge, not just its dictionary meaning, against the sentence's intent.

context_html: The town paper's report on the ceremony noted that the mayor's speech <u>wrapped up</u> with a call for volunteers.
stem_md: Which choice best suits the article's formal register?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Wrapped up' is conversational — out of register in a newspaper report.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Finished off' is just as casual, with a violent shading besides.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Was done' is flat and informal, and weakens the sentence's structure.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Concluded' states the same fact in the neutral, formal register a news report uses.

why_correct_md: Match the diction to the **register** of the surrounding text — formal reporting takes 'concluded'.
why_tempted_md: The informal options are exactly how the sentence would be spoken aloud.
rule_md: Identify the passage's register first; then pick the word that belongs to it.

context_html: In the lab report's discussion section, the experiment's results were <u>super weird</u>, prompting a full review of the method.
stem_md: Which choice best matches the passage's formal tone?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Super weird' is casual slang — jarring inside a formal lab report.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Unexpected' states the same fact in the register a lab report uses.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Totally bizarre' swaps one informality for another.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Kind of strange' keeps the conversational hedge the context forbids.

why_correct_md: Word choice must match the **register** of the surrounding passage — formal here.
why_tempted_md: The informal options are vivid and natural in speech.
rule_md: Check the passage's tone before judging a word: formal context → formal diction.

context_html: The rain finally <u>stopped the players</u> returned to the field.
stem_md: Which choice corrects the fused sentence?

per_choice_rationale.A: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation at all — a fused sentence.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses trades the fused sentence for a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.C: A period ends the first complete thought and lets the second begin cleanly.
per_choice_rationale.D: The comma after 'players' punctuates nothing — the two clauses are still fused.

why_correct_md: Two independent clauses need a real boundary — here, a **period**.
why_tempted_md: Read quickly, 'the rain stopped the players' parses as one clause, hiding the seam.
rule_md: Find where one complete thought ends and the next begins; mark that seam with a period, semicolon, or comma + conjunction.

context_html: The museum galleries were packed<u>, we</u> headed to the sculpture garden instead.
stem_md: Which choice best repairs the comma splice?

per_choice_rationale.A: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses — this is a comma splice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Comma + the coordinating conjunction 'so' legally joins the clauses AND names the cause-effect link.
per_choice_rationale.C: Deleting the comma fuses the clauses — no boundary at all.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'However' is not a coordinating conjunction; it would need a semicolon before it.

why_correct_md: Comma + **coordinating conjunction** (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) is a legal clause joiner.
why_tempted_md: 'However' feels like a conjunction, but it's an adverb — the classic splice non-fix.
rule_md: Join independent clauses with comma + FANBOYS, a semicolon, or a period — never a bare comma.

context_html: Although the museum stayed open late<u>. Visitors</u> still missed the final exhibit.
stem_md: Which choice repairs the sentence boundary?

per_choice_rationale.A: The period strands 'Although the museum stayed open late' as a fragment — a subordinate clause cannot stand alone.
per_choice_rationale.B: A comma joins the introductory 'although' clause to the main clause it modifies.
per_choice_rationale.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on BOTH sides; the 'although' clause is dependent.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Although' already subordinates the first clause — adding 'and' doubles up the connectors.

why_correct_md: A subordinate ('although') clause attaches to its main clause with a **comma**, not a period.
why_tempted_md: Reading aloud, the pause after 'late' feels like a full stop.
rule_md: A clause starting with although/because/while cannot stand alone — join it with a comma.

context_html: <u>Walking to school, the rain soaked Jordan's backpack.</u>
stem_md: Which revision corrects the modifier error?

choices.label: As Jordan walked to school, the rain soaked his backpack.
Walking to school, the rain quickly soaked Jordan's backpack.
Walking to school, Jordan's backpack was soaked by the rain.

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Walking to school' has nothing to modify but 'the rain' — and rain doesn't walk.
per_choice_rationale.B: Rewriting the modifier as a clause with its own subject ('As Jordan walked') puts the walker in the sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: Adding 'quickly' changes nothing: the rain is still the one walking.
per_choice_rationale.D: Now the backpack is walking to school — the modifier still dangles.

why_correct_md: A modifier must attach to the noun that actually performs it — give 'walking' its walker, **Jordan**.
why_tempted_md: Every option reads smoothly until you ask WHO is walking.
rule_md: Ask who performs the opening modifier's action; that noun must come immediately after the comma (or be given its own clause).

context_html: The coach praised the team for practicing daily, playing fairly, and <u>that they communicated</u> clearly.
stem_md: Which choice keeps the series parallel?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'That they communicated' breaks the -ing pattern set by 'practicing' and 'playing'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Communicating' matches the two -ing verbs, keeping the series parallel.
per_choice_rationale.C: The infinitive 'to communicate' mismatches the -ing forms.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'They communicated' inserts a full clause where the series expects a single -ing verb.

why_correct_md: Items in a series must share one grammatical form — here the **-ing** form.
why_tempted_md: Each option is grammatical in isolation; only the series pattern exposes the mismatch.
rule_md: Match every item in a list to the form the first items establish (parallel structure).

context_html: The internship taught her to manage budgets, to draft reports, and <u>public speaking</u>.
stem_md: Which choice maintains parallel structure in the list?

per_choice_rationale.A: The noun phrase 'public speaking' breaks the 'to + verb' pattern set by 'to manage' and 'to draft'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'How public speaking works' is a clause, not the infinitive the series expects — and it changes the meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'She learned public speaking' inserts a whole new clause into a series of infinitives.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'To speak in public' matches 'to manage' and 'to draft' — three parallel infinitives.

why_correct_md: Every item in the series must repeat the established form — here, the **infinitive** ('to ___').
why_tempted_md: 'Public speaking' is a perfectly natural phrase on its own; only the series pattern exposes it.
rule_md: Match each list item to the grammatical form the first item establishes.

context_html: The pianist's technique is more polished than <u>the other finalists</u>.
stem_md: Which choice makes the comparison logical?

per_choice_rationale.A: As written, the sentence compares a TECHNIQUE to PEOPLE — apples to orchestra members.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Than the other finalists are' still measures the people, not their technique.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'That of the other finalists' compares technique to technique — like to like.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'The other finalists' were' garbles the grammar and shifts tense mid-comparison.

why_correct_md: Comparisons must pair like with like: technique vs **that of** the others.
why_tempted_md: The shorthand comparison is how people actually talk, so the mismatch hides.
rule_md: When comparing possessions or attributes, add 'that of' / 'those of' so both sides match.

context_html: The committee will meet <u>at 9 a.m. in the morning</u> on Thursday.
stem_md: Which choice cuts the repeated time reference?

choices.label: at 9 a.m. in the early morning

per_choice_rationale.A: 'a.m.' already MEANS morning — 'in the morning' repeats it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Reordering the phrases doesn't remove the repetition.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'At 9 a.m.' states the time once, completely.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Early' adds a third layer to the same redundancy.

why_correct_md: '**a.m.**' contains 'morning'; saying both is saying it twice.
why_tempted_md: The doubled phrase is common in speech, where redundancy aids the listener.
rule_md: Expand abbreviations mentally (a.m. = morning) to catch hidden repetition.

context_html: The twins wore <u>identical matching</u> costumes to the parade.
stem_md: Which choice eliminates the redundant description?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Identical' and 'matching' say the same thing — one of them is dead weight.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Identical' alone carries the full meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: Reversing the order keeps both redundant words.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Identically matching' fuses the two redundancies into one phrase.

why_correct_md: Two words with one meaning → keep **one**.
why_tempted_md: Doubling adjectives feels emphatic, as if two synonyms are stronger than one.
rule_md: Cut any word that repeats what a neighboring word already says.

context_html: Students <u>who are members of</u> the robotics club meet on Tuesdays.
stem_md: Which choice is most concise while preserving the meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Who are members of' is grammatical but spends four words on what one preposition can do.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Students in the robotics club' — same meaning, three words saved.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Happen to belong to' adds hedging the sentence never asked for.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'That are being members of' is both wordier and ungrammatical.

why_correct_md: The ACT rewards the **shortest choice that keeps the meaning** — here, 'in'.
why_tempted_md: The longer relative clause sounds more formal and 'complete'.
rule_md: Try replacing a relative clause with a single preposition; if nothing is lost, the preposition wins.

context_html: The committee reached a <u>consensus of opinion</u> after two hours of debate.
stem_md: Which choice is the most concise without losing meaning?

per_choice_rationale.A: A consensus IS an agreement of opinion — 'of opinion' repeats what the word already says.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consensus' alone carries the full meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Shared' stacks a third redundancy onto the phrase.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Unanimous' adds yet another layer of the same idea.

why_correct_md: The ACT rewards the **shortest** option that preserves the meaning — 'consensus' says it all.
why_tempted_md: Longer phrases feel more formal and thorough.
rule_md: Cut words that restate what another word already contains.

context_html: Each morning, she would <u>rise up</u> at dawn to water the garden.
stem_md: Which choice removes the redundant word?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Rise' already means to move up — 'up' repeats it.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Rise' alone carries the full meaning.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Upward' is the same redundancy in a longer word.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Get up to rise' says the same thing twice in two ways.

why_correct_md: The direction is **inside the verb**: rising is upward by definition.
why_tempted_md: 'Rise up' is common in speech and song, so it sounds idiomatic.
rule_md: Drop particles that repeat the verb's built-in direction (rise up, descend down, return back).

context_html: <u>Due to the fact that</u> the bridge was icy, the road crew closed it overnight.
stem_md: Which choice trims the wordy opener?

choices.label: In light of the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Due to the fact that' spends five words doing one word's job.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Because' states the cause directly.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In light of the fact that' is even wordier than the original.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Being that' is both nonstandard and no shorter in spirit.

why_correct_md: **Because** replaces the five-word scaffold with the one word it means.
why_tempted_md: The long phrase sounds official, which reads as 'more correct'.
rule_md: Swap wordy connectors for their one-word equivalents (due to the fact that → because).

context_html: The novel's final chapter<u>, which comes at the end of the book,</u> resolves the mystery.
stem_md: Which choice best trims the redundant clause?

choices.label: , which is located at the book's end,
, coming at the end of the book's final pages,

per_choice_rationale.A: A 'final chapter' by definition comes at the end — the clause adds nothing.
per_choice_rationale.B: Deleting the clause leaves 'The novel's final chapter resolves the mystery' — complete and tighter.
per_choice_rationale.C: Rewording the redundancy doesn't remove it.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'End of the book's final pages' doubles the redundancy it was meant to fix.

why_correct_md: When a clause restates what 'final' already means, the fix is **deletion**, not rephrasing.
why_tempted_md: Rewritten versions look like improvements because they change the words — but not the waste.
rule_md: If a modifier repeats information the noun already carries, delete it entirely.

context_html: The old stone bridge <u>goes over</u> the gorge at a height of ninety meters.
stem_md: Which choice is the most precise description of the bridge?

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Goes over' is vague — people go over bridges; bridges do something more specific.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Spans' is the precise verb for a structure stretching across a gap.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Sits over' suggests resting on top of something, not stretching across it.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Happens across' means to encounter by chance — bridges don't do that.

why_correct_md: Precision means the verb built for the job: a bridge **spans** a gorge.
why_tempted_md: 'Goes over' is technically true, and 'true enough' masquerades as 'precise'.
rule_md: Prefer the specific verb over a general verb + preposition when one exists.

context_html: The reason the trail closed <u>is because</u> erosion damaged the footbridge.
stem_md: Which choice corrects the wordy construction after 'reason'?

choices.label: is due to the fact that

per_choice_rationale.A: 'The reason is because' says 'reason' twice — 'because' already means 'for the reason that'.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Due to the fact that' swaps one redundancy for five words of another.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'On account of because' stacks two causal phrases — doubly redundant.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'The reason is that' states the cause once, cleanly.

why_correct_md: After 'the reason is', use **that** — 'because' would smuggle in a second 'reason'.
why_tempted_md: 'The reason is because' is extremely common in speech and sounds natural.
rule_md: Pair 'the reason' with 'that'; pair 'because' with a plain clause — never both.
